source.title: LF-Steering: Latent Feature Activation Steering for Enhancing Semantic Consistency in Large Language Models
source.authors: Jingyuan Yang; Rong-Zhi Li; Wei-Xuan Wang; Ziyu Zhou; Zhi-Yong Feng; Wei Peng

record.tranche_reason: The paper uses polysemanticity and sparse-autoencoder features to motivate its steering method, but it does not test the claim's neuron interpretability rates or explanation-validity versions. Its neuron-level comparison is a steering comparison using transformer hidden states.
record.gate_note: Table 3 reports a neuron-level (described in the text as hidden-state) steering comparison with feature-level steering. This is relevant context for the claim's subject, but it does not test any listed version. The layer-location accuracy and other steering results do not measure neuron interpretability or explanation validity.
record.test_reason: The paper assumes the polysemanticity of model components (citing Elhage et al. 2022) to motivate SAE feature-level steering. It never measures how many individual neurons are interpretable. It never audits neuron explanations or scores them on held-out activations. It does not examine InceptionV1 or neuron-based attribution graphs. All results report its own steering method's accuracy and consistency on LLaMA2-7B-Chat, so no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right but incomplete. The authors' main conclusion is that LF-Steering achieves state-of-the-art semantic consistency and task gains over component-level steering baselines (ActAdd, CAA, SCS) on NLU and NLG datasets. They also conclude it beats hidden-state ('neuron-level') steering, and has good locality on out-of-domain sets. They acknowledge single-layer steering may be a partial solution and propose multi-layer circuit steering.
record.recipe_differences: This paper steers SAE feature activations to improve semantic consistency; it does not reproduce neuron explanation auditing, pole-level job classification, or explanation scoring on held-out activations.
record.method_sensitivity: For the RobustBOOLQ steering experiment, performance changes with the feature-difference threshold and activation strength; accuracy declines at thresholds of 0.25 or higher and at an extreme activation strength such as α = 50.0.

fits_no_version.finding: On LLaMA2-7B-Chat, steering SAE features at the top-1 layer gives higher task accuracy than steering that layer's raw hidden-state vector on all five datasets. The gain is large on BOOLQ (66.40 vs 50.50) and Sport (64.43 vs 52.74) and small on MRPC (68.38 vs 68.13). NLG cosine consistency is mixed: lower on Sport (0.78 vs 0.79), higher on Capital (0.83 vs 0.76).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For semantic-consistency activation steering, SAE feature-level interventions outperform interventions on a layer's raw hidden-state vector. This is indirect evidence on whether the neuron/hidden-state basis is a less clean unit for control.

record.problems: The comparison is on one model. The paper's neuron-level condition steers top-layer hidden states rather than testing individual neurons, and the reported results do not assess neuron interpretability or held-out activation prediction. The paper acknowledges that its single-layer approach may be partial.
record.rows_left_out: Tables 1, 4, 5, and 6 and the remaining reported results concern the proposed steering method, its controls, or out-of-domain task performance, not neuron interpretability or any listed version. Results attributed to earlier work were not recorded as this study's own findings.

untested.parts: Interpretability shares across other dense and MoE models and scales.
Reinterpretation of canonical polysemantic neurons such as InceptionV1 cat/car via pose and recursive generalization.
Whether architecture, regularization and tools drive the interpretable-neuron share, including the InceptionV1-sized estimates.
Neuron-based attribution graphs explaining behaviour without a replacement model.
Whether explanations fitted to activating examples fail to predict firing.

record.verdict_notes: Polysemanticity is asserted from citations, not measured. The 'neuron-level' baseline steers a whole hidden-state vector, so it says nothing about individual-neuron interpretability. The Table 2 manual interpretations concern two SAE features, not neurons. Single model, preprint.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B pole-level shares and any analogous neuron-pole job counts.
Interpretability shares across models, architectures, and scales.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose detection, and recursive generalization.
Whether architecture, regularization, or tools explain neuron interpretability rates, and the stated InceptionV1-sized estimates.
Whether attribution graphs using model neurons explain behavior without a trained replacement model or its reconstruction error.
Whether explanations fit to activating examples fail to predict other firing contexts.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulated activations on new text.

rows.note: The paper's neuron-level method steers transformer hidden states; it does not report an individual-neuron interpretability test.
rows.check: This is the study's own method compared with a variant of itself (an ablation), not a test of the claim. 'Neuron-level' here means steering the whole top-1 layer hidden-state vector, not individual neurons. The same applies to every Table 3 row: T3-*-neuron-* and T3-*-feature-* for BOOLQ, SST2, MRPC, Sport and Capital.
